verdicts.label: Supported
verdicts.definition: Everything the claim states (which node or ID, which number, which time, which cause) is shown by the cited evidence or follows from it. An inferred claim is supported when the cited observations make it a reasonable inference, even if no single line says it.
verdicts.plain: The boxes show everything the sentence says.

verdicts.label: Partially supported
verdicts.definition: Part of the claim is shown by the cited evidence and part is not: a number, time, node, scope or cause goes beyond what the evidence shows, or the evidence fits the claim but the claim says more than it can show. Say which part is not backed.
verdicts.plain: The boxes show some of it, but a number, time, node or cause goes further.

verdicts.label: Unsupported
verdicts.definition: The cited evidence contradicts the claim, is about something else, or nothing relevant is cited. A reference to a node only (for example S-TUN-012) shows that the node exists and how it connects; it does not support a claim about alarms, changes, measurements or causes.
verdicts.plain: The boxes contradict it, are about something else, or nothing relevant is cited.

verdicts.label: Not verifiable
verdicts.definition: The evidence needed to judge is not available: a cited reference is missing, or its text was shortened or omitted and the missing part could decide the claim. If all the evidence is there and does not back the claim, that is unsupported, not this.
verdicts.plain: Evidence is missing or cut short, so you cannot tell.

rules: Judge only against the text of the references the claim cites. A fact that appears only under another reference does not count.
Use no outside knowledge. Do not judge whether the claim is true in the real world, only whether the cited evidence backs it.
Check numbers, IDs and times literally. If the claim changes one (another node, another time, another count), it is not fully supported.
A cited tool call (T1, T2, ...) counts only through the output printed for it. If that output does not contain the fact, the call does not support the claim.
A claim that something was absent (no changes, no maintenance, no alarms) is supported by a cited call whose output reports none for the same nodes and time window.

A claim marked observed must be visible in the evidence. A claim marked inferred needs cited observations that make it a reasonable inference. The stated root cause is a conclusion and is judged like an inferred claim.

glossary.text: Loss of signal on a transport link: nothing arrives, the sites behind it go down.
A transport link works but poorly (reduced capacity or errors).
A radio site cannot be reached. A symptom: the cause is elsewhere.
A site lost mains electricity and runs on its battery.
A site's battery is nearly empty (about 15 minutes left).
A power module in a site cabinet is faulty.
Radio capacity of a site is almost fully used (PRB utilisation above 85-90 %).
Many phones fail to set up a connection on a site.
The DNS service (name lookup) times out too often.
Cabinet temperature is high. Common and usually harmless.
Signal reflection on an antenna cable. Frequent and usually harmless.
A cabinet cooling fan runs slowly.
A cabinet door is open, usually a technician visit.
A router's processor load is high. Brief spikes are normal.
Share of time a cell was in service. Normal is 100 %.
Downlink data volume delivered to users, in megabytes per 15 minutes.
Share of connection set-ups that succeed. Normal is about 99-99.7 %.
Share of sessions that end abnormally. Normal is 0.4-0.8 %.
Average round-trip time in milliseconds. Normal is about 20-40 ms.
Share of radio resource blocks in use, i.e. how full the cell is.
Number of phones connected to a cell.
What a value normally is at the same time of day on earlier days of the same type.
The first time step at which a value left its baseline.
An alarm that has been raised and not yet cleared.
An alarm that has ended.
How many typical deviations a value is from its baseline. Above about 3.5 counts as unusual.
A radio site, e.g. S-TUN-004 (TUN, SAH, SFX, SUD are regions).
One cell (sector) of a site, e.g. C-SAH-007-1.
A transport link (fiber or microwave) that connects sites to the network.
An aggregation router that gathers several links.
A core network node (UPF, DNS, AMF).
T1, T2, ...: a tool call the agent made; its output is the evidence.
ALM-000472: one alarm.
CHG-2026-0044: one configuration change.
MW-0003: one planned maintenance window.
EVT-004: one external event (holiday, stadium event).
ALR-0037: one detector alert, a group of related anomalies.
ANM-000163: one detected anomaly on one KPI of one node.
